```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(targets)
library(survival)
library(ggplot2)
tar_source("R")
tar_load(c(characters, cox, enet, ph, cox_show_clock, cv_summary, deployed_name,
           calibration, bias, simulation, boot))

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      text = element_text(colour = "#1c1b18"), axis.text = element_text(colour = "#1c1b18"),
      panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.line = element_line(linewidth = 0.3),
      axis.ticks = element_line(linewidth = 0.3), legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#f4f1e8", colour = NA),
      plot.title.position = "plot"
    )
)
ink <- "#1c1b18"
pct <- function(x, digits = 0) sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f%%"), 100 * x)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
metric <- function(model, name, horizon = NA) {
  row <- cv_summary[cv_summary$model == model & cv_summary$metric == name &
                      (is.na(horizon) | cv_summary$horizon %in% horizon), ]
  row$mean[1]
}
overall <- survfit(Surv(time_hrs, dead) ~ 1, data = characters)
horizon <- horizon_hrs(characters)
finale <- summary(overall, times = horizon)
med <- summary(overall)$table
bias_naive <- bias[bias$analysis == "Naive", ]
bias_lm <- bias[bias$analysis == "Landmark at 10 h", ]
sim_naive <- simulation$results[1, ]
sim_td <- simulation$results[2, ]
```

## Summary

This is a rework of a course project I wrote in 2020. The question is the same: which
characteristics of a Game of Thrones character predict how long they stay alive on screen?
The answers are more modest than the first version claimed, and I think more interesting.

- Of `r nrow(characters)` characters, `r sum(characters$dead)` die. Half are dead within
  `r num(med[["median"]], 1)` hours of their first appearance, and a character introduced in
  the first episode has a `r pct(finale$surv)` chance of reaching the finale
  (95% CI `r pct(finale$lower)` to `r pct(finale$upper)`).
- Using only what is known when a character is introduced (sex, social status, occupation,
  faith, allegiance), survival is **only weakly predictable**. The best model reaches a
  cross-validated C-index of about `r num(max(cv_summary$mean[cv_summary$metric == "c_index"]))`.
  Being a woman, being highborn and backing the Starks help; following the Boltons or the
  Drowned God does not.
- The 2020 version's strongest predictors, *prominence* and *switching allegiance*, were
  artefacts. A character must stay alive to switch sides or to appear in many episodes, so
  both look protective by construction. Switching appears to cut the hazard of death by
  `r pct(1 - bias_naive$hr)`. A simulation in which switching has **no effect at all**
  shows the same analysis reporting a `r pct(1 - sim_naive$hr)` reduction.
- The model on the [web page](../) is the `r c(cox = "plain Cox", enet = "elastic-net Cox")[[deployed_name]]`
  model, chosen by cross-validated Brier score. It is exported as coefficients plus a baseline
  hazard, and a test asserts that the JavaScript on the page reproduces R's predictions.

## Data

The data are the *Game of Thrones mortality and survival dataset* by Reidar Lystad and
Benjamin Brown ([figshare](https://figshare.com/articles/Game_of_Thrones_mortality_and_survival_dataset/8259680/1)),
which extends to season 8 the data behind their paper
["Death is certain, the time is not"](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40621-018-0174-7)
(*Injury Epidemiology*, 2018). Every character who appears on screen is followed from their
first appearance until they die or the series ends.

**Time scale.** Time is hours of running time since the character's first appearance.
Characters still alive at the end of season 8 are right-censored. A character introduced in
episode one can be followed for `r num(horizon, 1)` hours; one introduced in season 8 for a
few hours at most. Censoring is therefore administrative and depends only on when the
character was introduced.

**Covariates.** Levels with fewer than `r MIN_LEVEL_N` characters are pooled into "Other",
and the most common level of each factor is the reference.

```{r data-table}
do.call(rbind, lapply(BASELINE_TERMS, function(term) {
  data.frame(
    Covariate = TERM_LABELS[[term]], Level = levels(characters[[term]]),
    Characters = as.vector(table(characters[[term]])),
    Deaths = as.vector(tapply(characters$dead, characters[[term]], sum))
  )
}))
```

## What was wrong with the 2020 version

| Problem | What it did | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `prominence` and `allegiance_switched` used as predictors | Both are computed from a character's whole run, so they leak the outcome | Removed from the predictive model; analysed separately [below](#the-trap-immortal-time) |
| "Elastic Net" was lasso | `cv.glmnet` ran at its default `alpha = 1` | Alpha tuned over a grid |
| Two penalised models from two CV runs | `lambda.1se` and `lambda.min` came from different random folds | One fit, fixed folds |
| One 75/25 split | With 90 test characters the AUC moves by ±0.1 on the seed alone | 20 × 5-fold cross-validation |
| AUC at a single time point only | No measure of calibration | C-index, time-dependent AUC, Brier score, calibration |
| The final model did not match the chosen formula | Allegiance was "the winner" and then dropped | One model, stated once |
| A plot of deaths had its labels swapped | Alive was labelled "Yes" | Fixed |

## Survival curves

```{r km-overall}
#| fig-cap: "Kaplan-Meier estimate for all characters, with 95% confidence band."
s <- summary(overall, censored = FALSE)
ggplot(data.frame(t = c(0, s$time), s = c(1, s$surv), lo = c(1, s$lower), hi = c(1, s$upper)),
       aes(t, s)) +
  geom_step(aes(y = lo), linetype = "dotted", colour = ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_step(aes(y = hi), linetype = "dotted", colour = ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_step(colour = ink, linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Hours on screen since introduction", y = "Still alive")
```

The curve drops fastest at the start: many characters are introduced only to be killed.

```{r km-by}
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Kaplan-Meier curves by sex, social status and allegiance (four largest named houses)."
km_frame <- function(term, keep = NULL) {
  d <- if (is.null(keep)) characters else characters[characters[[term]] %in% keep, ]
  fit <- survfit(Surv(d$time_hrs, d$dead) ~ droplevels(d[[term]]))
  curves <- km_by_group(fit)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(curves), function(g) {
    data.frame(panel = TERM_LABELS[[term]], group = g, t = curves[[g]]$time, s = curves[[g]]$surv)
  }))
}
curves <- rbind(km_frame("sex"), km_frame("social_status"),
                km_frame("allegiance", c("Stark", "Lannister", "Night's Watch", "Targaryen")))
ends <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(curves, list(curves$panel, curves$group), drop = TRUE),
                              function(g) g[nrow(g), ]))
ggplot(curves, aes(t, s, group = group, linetype = group)) +
  geom_step(colour = ink, linewidth = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = group), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.8, size = 3, colour = ink) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.22))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Hours on screen since introduction", y = "Still alive")
```

```{r logrank}
do.call(rbind, lapply(BASELINE_TERMS, function(term) {
  test <- survdiff(Surv(characters$time_hrs, characters$dead) ~ characters[[term]])
  df <- length(test$n) - 1
  data.frame(Covariate = TERM_LABELS[[term]], `Chi-squared` = round(test$chisq, 1), df = df,
             `Log-rank p` = format.pval(pchisq(test$chisq, df, lower.tail = FALSE), digits = 2),
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
```

Each covariate separates the curves on its own. The covariates are also tangled together
(most Night's Watch characters are lowborn men, for example), so the next step is a joint model.

## Cox model

```{r forest}
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-cap: "Hazard ratios from the unpenalised Cox model, with 95% intervals. Right of the line means dying sooner than the reference group."
hr <- hazard_ratios(cox)
hr$label <- hr$column
for (term in BASELINE_TERMS) hr$label <- sub(paste0("^", term), paste0(TERM_LABELS[[term]], ": "), hr$label)
hr$label <- factor(hr$label, levels = rev(hr$label))
ggplot(hr, aes(hr, label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, linewidth = 0.4, colour = ink) +
  geom_point(shape = 22, fill = ink, colour = ink, size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() + labs(x = "Hazard ratio (log scale)", y = NULL)
```

Reference character: a `r tolower(levels(characters$social_status)[1])`
`r tolower(levels(characters$sex)[1])` in a `r tolower(levels(characters$occupation)[1])`
occupation, of `r tolower(levels(characters$religion)[1])` faith and
"`r levels(characters$allegiance)[1]`" allegiance. Most intervals cross 1. With
`r sum(characters$dead)` deaths spread over `r length(cox$coef)` coefficients, that is expected.

### Is the proportional-hazards assumption reasonable?

```{r ph}
transform(ph, chisq = round(chisq, 1), p = format.pval(p, digits = 2))
```

Not entirely. The global Schoenfeld test rejects, driven mainly by social status and occupation:
their effects change over a character's run. I keep the proportional-hazards form for the
deployed model because it has to be exported as a handful of numbers, and I judge the models
on Brier score and calibration, which do not assume it. The random forest below makes no such
assumption and serves as a check on how much is lost.

### Does the choice of clock matter?

Time since introduction is one choice. The other is the show's own clock, with each character
entering the risk set when introduced (left truncation), which compares characters who are
alive at the same point in the story.

```{r clocks}
#| fig-cap: "Coefficients under the two time scales. Points on the diagonal are identical."
both <- data.frame(character = cox$coef, show = coef(cox_show_clock)[names(cox$coef)])
ggplot(both, aes(character, show)) +
  geom_abline(linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink) +
  geom_point(shape = 22, fill = ink, colour = ink) +
  labs(x = "Coefficient, character clock", y = "Coefficient, show clock") + coord_equal()
```

The two agree closely (correlation `r num(cor(both$character, both$show))`), so the conclusions
do not hinge on the clock.

## Penalised Cox and a random forest

The elastic net shrinks the coefficients towards zero, trading a little bias for less variance.
Alpha is tuned over `r paste(ENET_ALPHAS, collapse = ", ")` and lambda by 10-fold
cross-validated partial likelihood, with the same folds for every alpha.

```{r enet}
transform(enet$tuning, cv_deviance = round(cv_deviance, 4))
```

The deviance barely moves across alpha: the data do not say whether ridge or lasso is better.
The chosen alpha is `r enet$alpha`.

```{r shrink}
#| fig-cap: "Elastic-net coefficients against unpenalised ones. Everything is pulled towards zero."
ggplot(data.frame(cox = cox$coef, enet = enet$coef), aes(cox, enet)) +
  geom_abline(linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.2, colour = ink) +
  geom_point(shape = 22, fill = ink, colour = ink) +
  labs(x = "Cox coefficient", y = "Elastic-net coefficient") + coord_equal()
```

The random survival forest (500 trees, minimum node size 15) can capture interactions and
non-proportional effects that the Cox models cannot.

## Validation

All figures below come from 20 repeats of stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Within a repeat,
every character is predicted by a model that never saw them; tuning happens inside each
training fold. The table shows the mean over repeats and the range covering 95% of them. That
range reflects the luck of the fold split, not sampling uncertainty in the data, which is larger.

```{r metrics}
wide <- function(name, digits = 3) {
  d <- cv_summary[cv_summary$metric == name, ]
  d$cell <- sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f (%.", digits, "f to %.", digits, "f)"), d$mean, d$lo, d$hi)
  d$Measure <- switch(name,
    c_index = "C-index", auc = paste0("AUC at ", d$horizon, " h"),
    brier = paste0("Brier at ", d$horizon, " h"), ibs = "Integrated Brier, 0 to 50 h")
  out <- reshape(d[c("Measure", "model", "cell")], idvar = "Measure", timevar = "model", direction = "wide")
  names(out) <- sub("^cell\\.", "", names(out))
  out
}
tab <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, all = TRUE, sort = FALSE),
              lapply(c("c_index", "auc", "ibs", "brier"), wide))
cols <- intersect(c("Measure", "Null model", "cox", "enet", "rsf"), names(tab))
tab <- tab[cols]
names(tab) <- c(Measure = "Measure", `Null model` = "No covariates", cox = "Cox",
                enet = "Elastic net", rsf = "Random forest")[cols]
tab[is.na(tab)] <- ""
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE)
```

Higher is better for C-index and AUC; lower is better for Brier. Three things stand out.

1. **The signal is weak.** A C-index near `r num(metric("enet", "c_index"))` means the model
   ranks a random pair of characters correctly a bit more often than a coin. Sex, status, faith
   and allegiance tell you something about who dies, but the writers decide most of it.
2. **Unpenalised Cox barely beats ignoring the covariates** on the integrated Brier score
   (`r num(metric("cox", "ibs"), 3)` against `r num(metric("Null model", "ibs"), 3)`), and by
   50 hours it is worse: its 18 coefficients overfit. Shrinkage helps
   (`r num(metric("enet", "ibs"), 3)`).
3. **The forest is a little better again** (`r num(metric("rsf", "ibs"), 3)`), which fits the
   proportional-hazards violation above. The gap is small next to the cost of shipping a forest
   to a browser, so the `r c(cox = "Cox", enet = "elastic-net")[[deployed_name]]` model is the one deployed.

```{r calibration}
#| fig-cap: "Calibration of the deployed model at 30 hours: out-of-fold predicted risk of death in five groups against the observed (Kaplan-Meier) risk."
ggplot(calibration, aes(predicted, observed)) +
  geom_abline(linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0, linewidth = 0.4, colour = ink) +
  geom_point(shape = 22, fill = ink, colour = ink, size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Predicted risk of death by 30 h", y = "Observed risk") + coord_equal()
```

The model's predicted risks span a narrow range, which is what an honest weak model should do,
and the groups sit near the diagonal.

## The trap: immortal time {#the-trap-immortal-time}

The 2020 analysis found that characters who switched allegiance lived much longer, and built
its final model on that. The effect is real in the data:

```{r bias}
knitr::kable(transform(bias, hr = round(hr, 2), lo = round(lo, 2), hi = round(hi, 2)),
             col.names = c("Analysis", "Hazard ratio for switching", "Lower", "Upper", "Characters", "Deaths"))
```

But "ever switched" is only known at the end of a character's run. Someone who dies in their
first scene never had the chance to switch, so they are counted as loyal, and all of the time
a switcher spent alive *before* switching is credited to switching. That stretch is called
immortal time: by definition, nobody dies in it.

A **landmark analysis** removes part of this. It keeps only characters still alive at a fixed
point (say 10 hours in) and restarts the clock there, so the early deaths no longer count
against the loyal. The hazard ratio moves from `r num(bias_naive$hr)` to `r num(bias_lm$hr)`,
and its interval now reaches 1. This is not a correction. The flag still includes switches
made after the landmark, and the dataset does not record when a switch happened.
**The true effect of switching sides cannot be estimated from this data.**

What can be shown is that the mechanism alone is enough to produce the result. In the
simulation below, `r format(simulation$n, big.mark = ",")` characters die at random and switch
sides at random, independently. Switching has no effect on anyone's hazard.

```{r simulation}
#| fig-cap: "Simulated data in which switching does nothing. Grouped by 'ever switched', the switchers still appear to live far longer."
sim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(simulation$curves), function(g) {
  data.frame(group = c(No = "Never switched", Yes = "Ever switched")[[g]],
             t = simulation$curves[[g]]$time, s = simulation$curves[[g]]$surv)
}))
ggplot(sim, aes(t, s, linetype = group)) + geom_step(colour = ink, linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Hours", y = "Still alive", linetype = NULL)
knitr::kable(transform(simulation$results, hr = round(hr, 2), lo = round(lo, 2), hi = round(hi, 2)),
             col.names = c("Analysis of the simulated data", "Hazard ratio", "Lower", "Upper"))
```

The naive analysis reports a hazard ratio of `r num(sim_naive$hr)` for something that does
nothing. Treating the switch as a time-dependent covariate, so that a character counts as a
switcher only from the moment they switch, recovers the truth
(`r num(sim_td$hr)`, interval `r num(sim_td$lo)` to `r num(sim_td$hi)`).
The same reasoning applies to `prominence`, which is built from the number of episodes a
character survived to appear in.

Dating each of the 55 switches from the episodes would allow the time-dependent analysis on
the real data. That is the natural next step.

## Limitations

- **Allegiance is the last known one**, not the one at introduction. For the 55 characters who
  switched, the model is told where they ended up. This is a milder form of the same leak and
  the data offer no way round it.
- **Small groups.** Several levels have 13 or 14 characters. Their coefficients are uncertain,
  and the penalty pulls them towards zero.
- **Proportional hazards does not hold** for every covariate.
- **Intervals on the web page** come from 200 bootstrap refits at fixed alpha and lambda. They
  leave out tuning uncertainty and are narrower than a fully honest interval would be.
- **This describes a script, not a population.** Deaths are authored. The model is for
  entertainment and for teaching survival analysis.
